description: AetherNova is driven by curiosity, innovation, and a passion for exploring the unknown. We aim to transform NASA's Earth data into meaningful insights using technology, data analysis, and creative problem-solving. Our mission is to explore challenges, discover patterns, and develop innovative solutions that make a difference. We believe every great discovery begins with curiosity and a willingness to learn. 🌎🚀
summary:
AetherNova is an interactive web application developed to explore and analyse rainfall patterns across Kerala using NASA Earth observation data. It uses NASA's GPM IMERG Final Precipitation V07 dataset to examine monthly rainfall, seasonal variations, anomalies, and long-term trends.

The application combines geospatial masking to focus on Kerala's land area with statistical methods such as the Mann–Kendall trend test and Sen's slope estimator. Through interactive visualisations, users can explore rainfall patterns, compare seasons, and understand changes over time. It also includes a spatial view of rainfall across 320 terrestrial grid cells and a June 2024 comparison with IMD reference data.

AetherNova addresses the challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” by transforming satellite precipitation data into accessible insights. It aims to support climate awareness and a better understanding of regional rainfall variability, while highlighting the importance and limitations of satellite-based observations.
details:
AetherNova – Kerala Rainfall Trend Detective

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

AetherNova is an interactive web application designed to analyse and visualise rainfall patterns across Kerala using NASA satellite precipitation data. It uses NASA's GPM IMERG Final Precipitation Level 3, Monthly V07 dataset.

The application processes monthly rainfall observations, applies a geographical boundary mask to focus on Kerala's land area, and uses cosine-latitude weighting for area-weighted rainfall calculations. It provides interactive visualisations of annual rainfall, seasonal patterns, rainfall anomalies, and spatial variations.

Statistical techniques, including the Mann–Kendall trend test, Sen's slope estimator, and linear regression, help users investigate rainfall trends and understand whether observed changes are statistically significant.

2. What are its benefits?

  • Makes NASA satellite rainfall data easier to explore and understand.
  • Helps identify seasonal rainfall variations and unusual rainfall patterns.
  • Provides interactive charts and spatial visualisations.
  • Supports climate awareness and educational research.
  • Demonstrates how Earth observation data can be transformed into meaningful information.

3. What is the intended impact?

AetherNova aims to make satellite-based rainfall analysis more accessible and encourage a better understanding of Kerala's rainfall behaviour. It can serve as an educational and analytical tool for students, researchers, and people interested in climate and environmental studies. It also demonstrates the potential of NASA Earth observation data in regional climate analysis.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

Programming languages: Python

Libraries and frameworks: Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pyMannKendall, Plotly, Shapely, xarray, and netCDF4.

Data sources: NASA GPM IMERG V07 and geoBoundaries Kerala geographical boundary data. IMD Kerala and Mahe reference data were used for a June 2024 comparison.

Development tools: Antigravity IDE, GitHub, and Streamlit Community Cloud.

No specialised hardware was required; the project was developed using a personal computer.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of AetherNova is its combination of satellite data processing, geospatial analysis, statistical trend detection, and interactive visualisation in one web application. Its dual-data-mode design provides an authentic NASA data mode covering 2018–2024 and a clearly labelled synthetic multi-decadal prototype for demonstrating longer-term analysis.

The application also includes a Kerala-focused spatial view using 320 terrestrial grid cells, helping users explore geographical rainfall variations rather than relying only on statewide averages.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered data reliability, geographical accuracy, statistical validity, usability, and transparency. A Kerala land-boundary mask helps exclude ocean and neighbouring-state areas from the analysis. The application also distinguishes authentic satellite observations from synthetic demonstration data.

Limitations such as satellite resolution, complex terrain, differences between satellite estimates and ground observations, and the available historical data period were considered. These factors are important when interpreting rainfall trends responsibly.
